sections.body: Bình luận mới được duyệt Xem tất cả Thông tin tài khoản Đổi mật khẩu Tin đã lưu Tin đã xem Đăng xuất Chính trị Chính trị Thời sự Thời sự Thế giới Thế giới Kinh tế Kinh tế Đời sống Đời sống Sức khỏe Sức khỏe Giới trẻ Giới trẻ Giáo dục Giáo dục Du lịch Du lịch Văn hóa Văn hóa Giải trí Giải trí Thể thao Thể thao Công nghệ Công nghệ - Game Xe Xe Video Video Tiêu dùng Tiêu dùng Thời trang trẻ Thời trang trẻ Đóng menu Chào ngày mới Tin 24h Tin thị trường Tin 360 Video Magazine Tiện ích Bạn cần biết Liên hệ Thông tin toà soạn Liên hệ quảng cáo Công nghệ Galaxy Z Fold8 có gì khiến người dùng điện thoại quyết định lên đời ngay? Nguồn: Samsung 10/08/2026 09:00 GMT+7 Chia sẻ Chọn Báo Thanh Niên làm nguồn ưu tiên trên Google tìm kiếm. Xem hướng dẫn. BƯỚC 1 Nhấp vào nút "Thêm Thanh Niên trên Google" hoặc mở trực tiếp đường dẫn này: https://www. google. com/preferences/source? q=thanhnien. vn BƯỚC 2 Tại trang vừa mở, tìm dòng "Báo Thanh Niên " và bấm vào ô vuông bên phải. Khi ô vuông chuyển thành dấu tích xanh là bạn đã thành công rồi! LƯU Ý NHỎ: Nếu muốn kiểm tra xem cài đặt còn hiệu lực không, bạn chỉ cần mở lại link trên là thấy ngay dấu tích xanh vẫn đang hiển thị. Chúc bạn đọc báo vui vẻ! --> Đã hài lòng với Galaxy Z Fold7 trong công việc hằng ngày, bác sĩ Vũ Trung Kiên không có ý định nâng cấp điện thoại sớm. Tuy nhiên, Galaxy Z Fold8 vẫn khiến anh quyết định đặt cọc sớm sau khi ra mắt nhờ những thay đổi đánh trúng nhu cầu sử dụng thực tế. Tín hiệu từ Thanh Nien Cong Nghe cần được đặt vào bối cảnh trước: thời điểm xuất hiện, chi tiết đã có cơ sở và lý do nó đáng nằm trong dòng tin công nghệ hôm nay. Phần này cần dựng lại thay đổi đã có cơ sở trước khi chuyển sang nhận định.

sections.heading: Tác động thực tế với người đọc
sections.body: Đối với bác sĩ Vũ Trung Kiên, người điều hành một phòng khám nha khoa tại Hà Nội, điện thoại không đơn thuần là thiết bị liên lạc mà đã trở thành một công cụ phục vụ công việc hằng ngày. Tác động thực tế nằm ở workflow, chi phí, rủi ro hoặc quyết định mua/dùng; Galaxy Z Fold8 có gì khiến người dùng điện thoại quyết định lên đời ngay? nên được giải thích qua lăng kính đó trước khi kết luận rộng hơn. Phần này cần nối câu chuyện với workflow, chi phí, bảo mật hoặc quyết định dùng/mua của người đọc.

sections.heading: Chi tiết cần kiểm chứng
sections.body: Trong các buổi tư vấn chỉnh nha, anh thường chụp cận cảnh khoang miệng để giúp khách hàng hình dung rõ tình trạng răng và hướng điều trị ngay từ những phút đầu tiên. Trước đây, việc này đòi hỏi khá nhiều thiết bị: chụp bằng máy ảnh DSLR, chuyển ảnh sang laptop rồi kết nối với TV để giải thích cho khách hàng. Câu hỏi tiếp theo là tín hiệu này có thành rollout bền vững, thay đổi giá trị sản phẩm, giới hạn đáng chú ý hay chỉ là một nhịp cập nhật ngắn. Phần này chỉ giữ chi tiết có thể kiểm chứng và tránh lặp lại nguyên văn cách diễn đạt của nguồn.

sections.heading: Ai nên hành động hoặc chờ
sections.body: Từ khi chuyển sang Galaxy Z Fold4, toàn bộ quá trình được rút gọn vào thiết bị duy nhất. Anh có thể trao đổi trực tiếp với khách hàng ngay trên điện thoại: "Đó là lần đầu tiên tôi cảm thấy một chiếc điện thoại thực sự giúp mình làm việc hiệu quả hơn, và cũng là lý do tôi gắn bó với Galaxy Z Fold đến tận bây giờ" . Với người đọc, khung hữu ích gồm bằng chứng hiện có, nhóm bị ảnh hưởng, rủi ro còn lại và điểm nên kiểm tra trước khi hành động. Phần này cần gọi đúng nhóm độc giả nên hành động ngay hoặc nên chờ thêm xác nhận.

sections.heading: Điều cần theo dõi tiếp
sections.body: Anh Kiên cho biết bản thân rất thực dụng khi quyết định nâng cấp: "Điện thoại gập không phải một sản phẩm rẻ, nên tôi càng không có lý do gì để nâng cấp chỉ vì có phiên bản mới. Nếu một thế hệ mới chưa giúp mình làm việc hiệu quả hơn thì tôi sẽ tiếp tục dùng chiếc máy cũ". Một bài tốt cần tách rõ sự kiện từ nguồn, tác động với người đọc và câu hỏi theo dõi để không giống bản tóm tắt link rời. Phần này nên khép lại bằng tín hiệu cần kiểm tra tiếp, không tóm tắt lại cùng một ý.

Khi mở ứng dụng trên những thiết bị này, người dùng sẽ nhận được thông báo yêu cầu "Switch to YouTube.com" (Chuyển sang YouTube.com). Điều đó đồng nghĩa người dùng chỉ có thể xem YouTube thông qua trình duyệt web thay vì ứng dụng cài sẵn.

Google cho biết việc ngừng hỗ trợ không đồng nghĩa Google Play Services sẽ bị gỡ khỏi điện thoại. Bộ dịch vụ này vẫn tồn tại trên thiết bị, tuy nhiên sẽ không còn nhận các bản cập nhật nền, API mới hay các bản vá bảo mật.

Điều đáng lo ngại là Google Play Protect - công cụ quét mã độc tích hợp trên Android sẽ không còn được cập nhật cơ sở dữ liệu mới. Điều này khiến thiết bị khó phát hiện các mối đe dọa bảo mật mới và có nguy cơ trở thành mục tiêu của tin tặc.

draft_context.source_title: Unveiling good and bad behaviors on the Agentic Internet
draft_context.description: The Internet isn’t a single lane of traffic. For a long time, the rule of thumb in web security was that bots are bad, while humans are good. Of course, we’re far past this generalization. Humans can be fraudulent, and bots can be helpful at different levels. Site owners actively want some automated traffic to interact with our sites to make the Internet functional and discoverable. To complicate things further, the line between "human" and "bot" is blurring more and more. Now, we have a type of “hybrid” traffic where a single session shifts from human to agentic and back again. (Think of a user browsing a store, and then handing off the checkout process to an automated shopping assistant.) So, how do website owners manage this kind of complexity? What matters here is assessing behaviors . Is this behavior abusive? Malicious? What’s the risk presented here, and can I trust this visitor based on their actions? Solving this requires moving beyond static, point-in-time checks. It requires analyzing continuous behaviors to evaluate Trust. In this post, we’ll share an inside look into the strategy of the Web Integrity & Trust team (covering the bots and fraud problem spaces) around detecting and analyzing good and bad behaviors, providing tools to help site owners tackle emerging challenges in the shifting Agentic Internet. We’ll also share findings around agentic traffic since the launch of Precursor , and a simulation where you can see how your own cursor movements would be assessed as human or bot — plus some exciting launch updates to expect in the near future. Defining Risk and Trust Let’s talk about the distinction between Risk and Trust , the way we discuss it within the teams at Cloudflare who work in bot detection. These are often viewed as polar opposites of a continuum. At Cloudflare, we look at them as independent, but reciprocal, values. Trust is the essential ingredient in making informed decisions on what to do about your traffic. Risk is how likely something like a request or action is to be harmful, and it’s often ephemeral. Trust, however, is built up over time, and it’s based on reputation. We can illustrate this with an example from real life: say that you’re enjoying some evening television at home, when suddenly, you hear the doorbell being rung repeatedly. Besides being annoying, this behavior is strange. Frantic doorbell rings late at night are alarming. You check through your door camera and see that the person ringing your doorbell is your best friend who lives next door. Of course, you trust your best friend, and we’d bet you would let them in. In this example, it wouldn’t be enough for you to say, “Reject anyone who rings my doorbell at night” or “Reject anyone who rings my doorbell more than 10 times.” Again, Trust is the essential ingredient. Going back to traffic on the Internet, the strategy as we build products in the bots and fraud space focuses on building an entire ecosystem based on Trust. And our goal is to provide the incentives and primitives for site owners to use to incentivize behavior that makes the Internet safer for everyone: starting with blocking malicious activity at the bottom, to encouraging participation in a safer Internet at the top. Good behaviors, rooted in transparency Starting at the top: what counts as good behavior? We can draw clear examples from the Verified bots and agents within BotBase. Last month, we announced an updated pragmatic taxonomy for the good bots we track in our system , boiling down the definition of “ Verified ” to two things: 1) you declare yourself honestly, and 2) you don’t abuse the trust you’ve earned. Transparency between a site owner and a bot operator allows for a symbiotic relationship: site owners can note what behaviors and data uses they want to allow on their websites, and bot operators can be granted access more easily. The transparency allows for Trust in the relationship; if you have nothing to hide, declaring who you are should reduce friction from the sites who want to allow your behaviors. BotBase is not meant to only make declarations of “who is good”. It is intended to be a directory of all known bots and agents, and provide the facts. Compared to our previous Bots Directory, which only included known good bots, BotBase is also capable of tracking less-than-good bots and agents. Why? Because our systems track and validate behavior for known good actors, meaning we have the tools to identify when these expectations aren’t met. If you abuse trust on the Cloudflare network, you should not be easily allowed, so you will be unverified. Bad behaviors: blatant, stealthy, and everything in between A few weeks ago, we announced Precursor , a continuous client-side system to detect even subtly inhuman bot traffic that can fly under the radar when assessing network signals alone. When a customer enables Precursor, the JavaScript detection is CDN-injected, so it doesn’t require sitting at the computer and figuring out where or how to rerun these detections. What's more, Precursor evaluates user behavior continuously throughout the session , so no more free hall passes for abusive traffic that found a way to pass client and browser-side checks just once. Applying our Risk and Trust framework to these client-side detections, we can point out that CAPTCHAs or one-time hurdles are Risk-based, meaning they lack context . On the other hand, verification using behavioral tells is Trust-based, since it can capture more context clues from the full user session. Precursor is the tool for us to analyze this behavior. To sum it up, Precursor is so powerful because it: Provides Trust-based detection over the entire user session. Drives up the cost for bot developers to replicate human behavior over a multipage timeline. By making it economically disadvantageous for bot developers to outrun these detections, we win the adversarial game. Now, what have we learned since we’ve launched? Looking at just a 24-hour period at the time of writing this blog, we can see 206 million Precursor evaluation events , across 73,438 zones on the Cloudflare network. We can see patterns in the data that reveal things that we had suspected when launching the detection, but can now validate across tens of thousands of domains: Suspicious behavior often happens mid-session, which point-in-time detection wouldn’t catch. Behavior often shifts from human to agentic and back over a session . In these cases, it’s important to understand the intent so that site owners don’t block user flows that they actually want. This highlights the importance of a bot classification system that allows website owners to handle traffic by use case, purpose, and data use. This is precisely why we prioritized taxonomy updates for BotBase. For those curious to learn more on how Precursor actually works, we shared a sneak peek — how the signals we analyze showed us that to err is human — in our announcement blog post . Today, we’re going a step further: giving anyone on the Internet an interactive demo simulating how Precursor would trace your cursor movements. Precursor Trace is live now, sharing how we’d assess your cursor movements using (part of) Precursor’s detection mechanism. Here, you can see whether you’re accelerating or correcting yourself, the rhythm and texture of your cursor movement, and more — all things you’ve probably never thought about as a real human being interacting with a computer. Try it out! Adaptive Intelligence is coming soon Cloudflare’s bot detection engines can produce different outcomes when assessing if a given request is automated or not. For requests that are deemed to be automated, the assessment can be 1) definitely automated, based on proven, deterministic methods or fingerprints of bots, or 2) likely automated, based on predictive scoring from Cloudflare’s Bots ML. Historically, Bots ML has been updated in versions, meaning we announced each new model version as a product launch. This pacing doesn’t work when bots adapt on the scale of hours or even minutes. Adaptive Intelligence, a completely new detection engine, is different from anything we’ve built before in the Bots ML space. The model itself is adaptive . It has learned from everything we’ve seen in the past, but more importantly, it will continue to learn and self-adjust based on what it sees. Adaptive Intelligence will upgrade itself based on a wide range of traffic patterns we identify, from good to bad behaviors, and customers will no longer need to upgrade to a formal new model version to have the latest predictive bot detections working for them. All Bot Management customers will have access to Adaptive Intelligence in the near future — stay tuned for the launch announcement coming soon. Moving beyond determinism to influence bot behavior So far, we’ve focused on Cloudflare’s side of things: strategy, detection, and taxonomy. All of this allows Cloudflare to equip website owners with the tools they need to set the traffic policies they want on their sites. Zooming in on the website owner side, we want to take this chance to discuss some advanced mitigations that allow website owners themselves to influence bot behavior. With more blatant mitigation techniques, we face something that we’ve nicknamed the “Bot Antibiotic Problem.” Always sending bots a deterministic response (like a 403 block) makes it easy for a malicious developer bot to probe, observe, and reverse-engineer your defenses. We know this, so we’re designing mitigations specifically made for throttling bots — with different approaches for malicious bots vs. benign bots. We can break them down into three approaches: Approach 1: Unpredictability and Random Actions. Applying random responses (between block, challenge, or allow) to suspected automated traffic breaks a bot's automated retry logic and fingerprinting. Approach 2: AI Labyrinth , a defensive response that traps unauthorized bots in an endless maze of AI-generated web pages. You can waste malicious bots' compute and crawl budgets by using misdirection . Site owners will be given three options within AI Labyrinth, depending on their preference: Maze : Generates an endless web of linked pages for bots to follow. Summary : Feeds crawlers an LLM-generated summary of a page that looks real but is entirely useless as AI training data. Poison : Serves deliberately fake content (like fake prices or inventory) to a bot, polluting the data it collects for AI training. Approach 3: Queuing for Good Bots. Not all agentic traffic is bad; queuing manages throughput for legitimate automated traffic (like user-directed shopping agents) without denying them service entirely. These advanced, bot-specific mitigations are set to roll out closer towards the end of the year, and will be available for the website owner to choose how strict they want their mitigations to be. We also know that a great defense is a predictive one — one that self-learns and course-corrects without needing multiple security experts on a call to reactively set a fix that accounts for the latest stealth attack. This might look like having a system of “disposable” rules, in which the ruleset is dynamic in nature. This is by design: if attacks constantly evolve, the defenses should, too. That’s why we’re working to keep both detections and mitigations a step ahead. Establish the Trust ecosystem that works for you Anyone and everyone can take steps to define how automated agents interact with their infrastructure. A few things to try: Turn on Precursor Play around with Precursor Trace Explore BotBase By moving away from static, point-in-time checks and embracing continuous trust evaluation, we reduce the game of whack-a-mole with bot operators. If you’re not already using Cloudflare’s bot detection , check it out and establish the Trust ecosystem that works for you.

sections.heading: Practical impact for readers

Especially as the company doesn’t gouge you for IP cam licenses. NAS requires a bit more tech savvy than cloud services and storage, plus some upfront cost, but there’s one particular reason it’s worth it: complete and private control of the apps, services, and most importantly –the data you store on it. Internet outage? Doesn’t affect your NAS. Online data breech? Doesn’t affect your NAS. Monthly payments? Only to your power company. Simply put, NAS is fantastic for data backup and streaming media about the house and can also serve as the engine for a home surveillance network. We like NAS, and TerraMaster has quickly become one of our favorite consumer flavors thanks to excellent hardware and apps, a newly faster OS, and the lack of surcharges vendors such as QNAP and Synology hit you up with for things such as additional IP cam licenses. That said, there was the occasional immaturity in the apps and operating system. What are the F4-425 Pro’s features? The F4-425 Pro is a silver and black hued, mostly metal, four-bay NAS box with quick swap, non-locking 3.5-inch drive trays. It measures approximately 7.1-inches wide by 8.6-inches deep, by 5.9-inches tall and weighs around 6.5 pounds bare. That will of course increase as you add drives. If you remove the four screws on the bottom holding the aluminum body to the chassis, you’ll find three PCIe 3.0 NVMe M.2 slots that accept NVMe SSDs. There’s enough space for heat sinks, which would be a good idea to prolong SSD life. Note that you can use PCIe 4.0/5.0 SSDs but they’ll be limited to PCIe 3.0 speed. The front of the unit provides access to the four drive bays, as well as the power button and a single 10Gbps USB Type-A port. The back is home to an additional pair of 10Gbps Type-A USB ports, twin 5Gbe Ethernet ports, and HDMI port (console use only), and a single Type-C port for diagnostics and the like. There’s also the power jack, a pinhole reset button, and a rather massive exhaust fan. The back of the F4-425 Pro with its dual 2.5Gbpe and 10GBps Type-A ports. There’s a Type-C port but it’s only for diagnostics. The HDMI port is for console (command prompt) use only. The processor inside of our test unit was a capable 8-core Intel N350 with a substantial 16GB of DDR5 onboard. That’s plenty of power for advanced tasks like virtual machines and Docker. TerraMaster also provides several apps for backup up mobile devices, and even controlling the box. The TNAS mobile app on install and first use. TerraMaster provides 2-year warranty on the F4-425 Pro. And thankfully, the company now also provides a downloadable PDF user’s guide. How is the F4-425 Pro’s setup? Adding drives to the tool-less trays is largely painless: slide them out, pop out the side rails, slip in the 3.5-inch HDD and replace the side rails. Screws are provided for 2.5-inch hard drives or SATA SSDs. As described above, you’ll need to remove the outer shell to access the three PCIe 3.0 NVMe slots. lWhen you first boot the F4-425 (and most TerraMaster NAS) it presents a dialog asking for your email address to receive a code. That’s of course after you find its IP address (E.g. 192/168.1.110) and visit with your browser. Below the email field, in very light lettering, is the ability to bypass this step. If you choose, you can activate your online presence with TerraMaster during setup. Alas, you still have to enter your email. I don’t like sending info to a company until I’m very familiar with the hardware and said company. I wish TerraMaster would abandon this practice ad to be blunt–it’s none of their darn business. To be fair, you can put the F4-425 Pro into “Security Isolation Mode” (Control Panel / Security/ Security Isolation Mode) after setup, to prevent any further traffic outside of your local network. The F4-425 also features a highly configurable firewall if that’s too drastic a measure for you. What is the F4-425 Pro’s operating system and software like? The F4-425 Pro delivered our first look at the latest version 7 of TOS (TerraMaster Operating System), a substantially feature-equivalent but far better-performing version of the operating system (version 6) than I tested with the F2-425 . Especially in regards multitasking. Beyond that, it appeared to me to be more evolutionary than revolutionary, despite heralding itself as the first AI-enabled NAS OS. It does allow you to install OpenCLAW which enables normal language access to various features. TerraMaster says OpenCLAW makes things easier, but the real issue with most new NAS users is that they don’t know what to ask, let alone how to ask it. Actually, thinking about it, that’s the issue with just about any AI system. Note also that the minute I opened OpenCLAW, the F4-425 Pro’s fan kicked into high gear. It takes some juice. That said, I quite like TOS, it’s as well laid out as the QNAP and Synology equivalents, and perhaps a bit more intuitive. However, I found version 7 a bit buggy. Rough around the edges, as it were. I stuck with TOS 7 as it’s so much quicker at everything than version 6 but there were some annoyances such as the inability to include spaces in a backup job name, and not automatically resuming jobs that were not completed in the last session. I’d also be careful doing searches and deleting the results with the file manager. There are also tons of apps for backup, surveillance, development, and multimedia streaming. Below is my favorite: Centralized Backup, which can back up from numerous sources (SMB, FTP, etc.) without the need to install clients on every machine. Simply share the folders or files you want across the network, locate them and create a job to back them up. I love Centralized Backup’s ability to back up my shared folders without me having to install client software on the involved computers. Centralized Backup, along with CloudSync (back up to a host of online services) are my favorite TOS backup apps, but there are quite a few others (Duple Vault, Elephant Drive, etc.) as well as TerraMaster’s own client-based, portal driven TerraSync. There’s also a handy folder mirroring utility (TFM) that you can use across volumes. eAll the backup and sync options offered by TOS 7. Want to keep tabs on your house? TerraMaster includes Surveillance Manager (shown below), which offers support for unlimited cameras. This is in distinct contrast to Synology and QNAP which limit you to one or two cameras so they can sell you more licenses. This is one of the best reasons to opt for a TerraMaster NAS box, however, note that you’ll have to configure your router to reach the app remotely. The Surveillance Manager opens in a separate tab and allows up to tk IP cams. While I use TOS’s DLNA Multimedia Server to stream movies to my TV, TerraMaster also includes the extremely popular Plex (shown below), as well as Jellyfin and Emby for fans of those systems. The extremely popular Plex Media Server is present in TOS 7. TRAID is TerraMaster’s hybrid RAID solution (all NAS vendors have one these days) that combines mirroring (RAID 1) and parity (RAID 5). It allows you to combine drives of different sizes while using more of their capacity than standard RAID modes do. Generally speaking, most RAID modes allow you to use only the capacity of each drive in the array equal to that of the smallest drive in the array. Combine a 4TB HDD and an 8TB HDD in RAID 0 (striping) or RAID 1 (mirroring), and only 4TB of the 8TB drive is used, while the rest just sits there. TRAID and similar solutions let you employ the otherwise wasted capacity as another volume, or part of one. How much is the F4-425? The F4-425 Pro with the Intel N350 retails for $799, but was on sale at TerraMaster’s site for $639 at the time of this writing. From TerraMaster’s Amazon store make that $699. There’s a cheaper $569 Intel N305/8GB version of the F4-425 Pro available, as well as less endowed $599 F4-425 Plus (Intel N150 processor, 16GB), and $429 F4-425 (quad-core, 4GB) models if the Pro is too pricey for you, or you don’t need to run VMs, Docker, etc. The Plus and plain versions were discounted to $480 and $344 respectively at the time of this writing. All use the same operating system and offer the same applications. The F4-425 Pro’s price is roughly on par for a NAS box with this grade of processor, 16GB of memory and NVMe slots, but as always — shop around, though we’re fairly sure you’d be happiest with the TerraMaster. How does the F4-425 perform? The F4-425 Pro features dual 5Gbpe (Multi-gig) so it’s capable of nearly 600MBps when using that protocol, and around 1GBps if you aggregate the two 5Gbps Ethernet adapters. At 2.5Gbps, expect around 290MBps, and on gigabit, around 140Mbps. There’s no Wi-Fi, but that’s not the best way to use a NAS box. You can with some (and an add-in card), but commonly NAS is connected via Ethernet directly to a router or switch. I populated the F4-425 with a single 1.92GB Seagate IronWolf SATA SSD and two Crucial T710 PCIe 5.0 NVMe SSDs (running at PCIe 3.0 speed) and formatted with the Btrfs file system. All those SSDs are massively faster than 5Gbpe or even 10Gbpe. The test network consisted of my M4 Max Studio, an EnGenius ECS2512FP 12-port switch (8 x 2.5Gbe/4 x 10Gbe), and PCWorld’s 10Gbe Intel testbed. I tested with both a single 5Gbe Ethernet connection and both 5Gbe Ethernet ports bonded using TOS 7. However, there was so little improvement with the ports bonded, I’m showing only the 5Gbe results. As to that… Disk Speed Test was quite complimentary of the F4-425’s throughput, and more so than AmorphousDiskMark. Disk Speed Test was complimentary of the F4-425’s throughput, and more so than AmorphousDiskMark. AmorphousDiskMark writes more data at a time than Disk Speed Test, which may be the reason for the lower write number. That said, CrystalDiskMark on the PC showed even greater performance that Disk Speed Test — 587MBps reading and 580GBps writing. AmorphousDiskMark writes more data at a time than Disk Speed Test, which may be the reason for the lower write number. That said, CrystalDiskMark on the PC showed even greater performance that Disk Speed Test — 587MBps reading and 470GBps writing. ATTO was more in line with Disk Speed Test than AmorphousDiskMark. ATTO was more in line with Disk Speed Test than AmorphousDiskMark. As to sprightlyness, I banged on the interface and apps pretty hard. The F4-425 Pro was extremely responsive. Tasks completely quickly, including firmware updates and reboots. The latter were far faster than what I’m used to with my older NAS boxes. Multi-tasking, which I complained about with TOS 6 on the F2-425 was light years better. Thank you TOS 7! And of course, more memory and a faster processor. TerraMaster’s advertising teases over 1GBps performance. However, that’s simply totaling two separate 500GBps connections working separately. Expect what you see above. Note also that there is a list of compatible NVMe SSDs found here . I’ve had issues with the F8 SSD Plus with some that weren’t supported, though the F4-425 seems fine with the same SSDs. I also found that some software required re-enabling after reboots or shutdowns in TOS 7. Should I buy the F4-425 Pro? If you need a very fast 4-Bay NAS box, the TerraMaster F4-425 fits the bill. Though you should expect a couple of software glitches here and there with TOS 7 that QNAP and Synology don’t suffer. That said, for creating a surveillance system, the lack of additional fees makes it top dog in that department.
